A1-A2.headline: How People Learned to Take Pictures

pages.text:
How did people learn to save a real moment in time? Photos need two simple ideas. Light sends a view, and a surface reacts to that light.

No proof shows people tried to save photos before the 1700s.
pages.caption: An early photographic wagon from 1855.

evidence.articleCaption: A salted paper print taken by Roger Fenton of his assistant and photographic wagon, 1855

pages.text:
Long before modern film, the camera obscura sent an upside-down view through a tiny hole onto a wall.

Early teachers used it to watch sun events safely. Later, artists used it as a handy drawing tool.
pages.caption: The simple principle of the camera obscura.

pages.text:
Early testers made real steps with things that react to light. Around 1718, Johann Heinrich Schulze used a silver mix to print cut-out letters. Still, those marks did not last long.

Around 1800, Thomas Wedgwood made light shadow prints on paper. Even so, he could not keep camera views fixed for good.

The big break came in 1826 or 1827. Nicéphore Niépce fixed a camera view after hours in the sun.

Later, his partner Louis Daguerre built a faster way. It took only minutes and gave sharp detail.
pages.caption: Daguerre's famous 1838 street view photo.

evidence.articleCaption: The Boulevard du Temple, Louis Daguerre's 1838 daguerreotype of a busy street, with only one man remaining in one place long enough to be clearly visible (near the bottom left corner).

pages.text:
At the same time, Henry Fox Talbot built a paper method called the calotype. New tools soon made cameras faster and easier to carry. Photo making spread fast around the world.

Late in the 1900s, digital cameras arrived. Soon, simple phone and digital cameras turned film photos into an everyday digital habit.

pages.text:
How did people learn to freeze a passing moment? Photography relies on two basic ideas: light projection and light-reactive materials.

No record shows anyone trying to fix camera views before the 18th century.
pages.caption: An assistant and photographic wagon photographed in 1855.

evidence.articleCaption: A salted paper print taken by Roger Fenton of his assistant and photographic wagon, 1855

pages.text:
Long before chemical film, the camera obscura cast a flipped image through a small hole onto a flat wall.

Scholars first used it to study light and watch solar eclipses safely. Later, artists used it for drawing.
pages.caption: The optical principle behind the camera obscura.

pages.text:
Early testers made clear gains with light-sensitive materials. Around 1718, Johann Heinrich Schulze used a silver paste to record stenciled letters, though the marks soon faded.

Around 1800, Thomas Wedgwood made shadow prints on treated sheets. Even so, he could not keep camera views fixed for long.

A real breakthrough came in 1826 or 1827. Nicéphore Niépce fixed a camera view after hours of light exposure.

Later, Louis Daguerre created the daguerreotype. It cut wait times to minutes with sharp detail.
pages.caption: Daguerre's 1838 daguerreotype of the Boulevard du Temple.

evidence.articleCaption: The Boulevard du Temple, Louis Daguerre's 1838 daguerreotype of a busy street, with only one man remaining in one place long enough to be clearly visible (near the bottom left corner).

pages.text:
Meanwhile, Henry Fox Talbot built a rival paper-negative method called the calotype. Later gains made film faster and easier to carry, so photography spread quickly.

In the late 20th century, digital cameras arrived. Over time, they turned film photography into a common digital medium.

C1-C2.headline: Historical Trajectories in the Chemical and Digital Capture of Light

pages.text:
How did humanity master arresting fleeting moments? Photography integrates two foundational principles: optical light projection and photosensitive chemistry.

No documentary evidence precedes the 18th century for fixing camera images.
pages.caption: A salted paper print captured by Roger Fenton in 1855.

evidence.articleCaption: A salted paper print taken by Roger Fenton of his assistant and photographic wagon, 1855

pages.text:
Centuries before chemical emulsions, the camera obscura projected inverted vistas through a pinhole aperture onto interior surfaces.

Initially utilized by savants investigating optics and solar eclipses, it subsequently aided painters.
pages.caption: Schematic representation of the camera obscura.

pages.text:
Pioneering investigators achieved incremental milestones with photosensitive compounds. Around 1718, Johann Heinrich Schulze utilized a silver-bearing suspension to record stenciled characters, though the impressions remained ephemeral.

Around 1800, Thomas Wedgwood fabricated photograms yet proved unable to permanently stabilize camera-projected imagery.

A pivotal breakthrough emerged in 1826 or 1827, when Nicéphore Niépce fixed a view after protracted exposure.

Following his demise, collaborator Louis Daguerre unveiled the daguerreotype, slashing exposure to minutes.
pages.caption: Louis Daguerre's 1838 daguerreotype of the Boulevard du Temple.

evidence.articleCaption: The Boulevard du Temple, Louis Daguerre's 1838 daguerreotype of a busy street, with only one man remaining in one place long enough to be clearly visible (near the bottom left corner).

pages.text:
Concurrently, Henry Fox Talbot devised an alternative paper-negative methodology termed the calotype. As subsequent photochemical refinements enhanced sensitivity and portability, photography proliferated globally.

During the late twentieth century, digital imaging sensors emerged, ultimately supplanting analog film with an omnipresent digital medium.
